title: The Polycrisis Bill
subtitle: What interacting crises are costing the world this century — an interactive ledger, 2025–2100
strapline: Every 1 per cent of world output lost each year this century adds up to about $260 trillion. Depending on what is counted, the polycrisis already costs between 1 and 23.5 per cent of output a year; on plausible paths the century's bill runs from hundreds of trillions to several quadrillion dollars — and prevention costs a fraction of it.
dek: Disasters, heat, pollution, violence and the climate damage locked in by each year's emissions already cost between 1.2 and 23.5 per cent of world output a year, depending on what is counted. Over 2025–2100 that adds up to hundreds of trillions to several quadrillion dollars, and prevention would cost a fraction of it.
abstract: This report estimates what the polycrisis — interacting crises in climate, pollution, health, conflict and ecosystems — is costing the world economy, and what it could cost by 2100. It begins with a ledger of published annual estimates: direct disaster losses of about $0.3 trillion (an average of $368 billion in 2024 and $224 billion in 2025), heat-related labour losses of $1.09 trillion (2024), air-pollution health damage of $8.1 trillion (2019), the non-military economic impact of violence, about 6.4 per cent of world output (2024), world military spending of $2.72 trillion (2024), and $8.0 trillion of future climate damage locked in each year by current emissions at the US EPA's social cost of carbon. These figures measure different things — lost output, welfare including lives, defensive spending, future liabilities — so they cannot simply be summed. Depending on which accounts are included, the annual cost ranges from about 1.2 per cent of 2025 world output ($1.4 trillion, market losses only) to 8 per cent with health, 14 per cent with violence and 23.5 per cent with security spending and accrued climate liabilities.

The losses are projected to grow. Swiss Re's stress test puts climate-related losses at 11 to 18 per cent of world output by 2050 in higher-warming scenarios; the World Bank projects antimicrobial resistance costing 1.1 to 3.8 per cent of output by 2050 and the collapse of selected ecosystem services $2.7 trillion a year by 2030. Some widely cited projections, including the 2024 NGFS damage estimates, rest on a study that has since been retracted, and are flagged accordingly.

A century calculator turns these shares into a bill. At 2.5 per cent real growth, world output between 2025 and 2100 totals about $26 quadrillion in 2025 dollars, so every percentage point of output lost each year costs about $262 trillion over the century. A central path in which losses rise from 4 to 10 per cent of output gives about $2.1 quadrillion undiscounted — $205 trillion in 2025–2049, $529 trillion in 2050–2074 and $1.33 quadrillion in 2075–2100 — or $781 trillion in present value at a 2 per cent discount rate. A low path (2 to 5 per cent) gives $1.0 quadrillion and a high path (8 to 20 per cent) $4.1 quadrillion. Commonly quoted ranges of $600 trillion to $3 quadrillion correspond to losing between 2.3 and 11.5 per cent of output every year.

Prevention is cheap by comparison. In the calculator, spending 1.5 per cent of output a year to avoid 40 per cent of losses, phased in over twenty years, returns about $2 for every $1 over the century and saves about $400 trillion net — a conservative result next to the Global Commission on Adaptation's benefit-cost ratios of 2 to 10. International adaptation finance, at $26 billion in 2023, meets less than a tenth of the $310–365 billion a year that developing countries need. The figures in this report are scenarios built from published estimates; they show orders of magnitude and the accounting choices that drive them, not forecasts.
jel: Q54, Q51, Q53, H56, I15, E01, D61 — climate and natural disasters; valuation of environmental effects; air pollution; national security and war; health and economic development; measurement of national income; cost–benefit analysis
method: World output is the World Bank's World Development Indicators estimate for 2025 (US$118.35 trillion, current prices). Ledger entries are published estimates in their own years: Munich Re natural catastrophe losses for 2024 (US$368 billion) and 2025 (US$224 billion), averaged; Lancet Countdown 2025 heat-related labour income loss for 2024 (US$1.09 trillion); World Bank health cost of PM2.5 air pollution for 2019 (US$8.1 trillion, 6.1 per cent of world GDP, a welfare measure including the value of lives); Institute for Economics and Peace Global Peace Index 2025 economic impact of violence for 2024 (US$19.97 trillion in purchasing-power terms, 11.6 per cent of gross world product, about 45 per cent military spending) — the non-military share, 6.4 per cent, is applied to 2025 world output to put it in market terms; SIPRI world military expenditure for 2024 (US$2.718 trillion); Newman and Noy (2023) climate-attributable extreme-weather costs, 2000–2019 average (US$143 billion a year); Global Carbon Budget 2025 total CO2 emissions (42.2 Gt) valued at the US EPA's 2023 social cost of carbon of US$190 per tonne (2 per cent discount rate); and the World Bank's projection of US$2.7 trillion a year in losses by 2030 from the collapse of selected ecosystem services. Ledger totals are shares of 2025 world output; entries are not adjusted for overlap, which is flagged where known. The century calculator assumes constant real growth g from US$118.35 trillion in 2025, a loss share that rises linearly from s0 in 2025 to s1 in 2100, and discounting at rate r; periods are 2025–2049, 2050–2074 and 2075–2100. The prevention calculator assumes prevention spending of c per cent of output each year avoids a fraction a of losses, phased in linearly over 20 years. All values are in 2025 US dollars at market exchange rates unless stated. Outputs are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts.
author: Hunter Hughes
